questions.q: State the precise definition of equal sets and equivalent sets for finite sets. Use mathematical notation (∈, n(A), etc.).
questions.a: Equal sets: A = B ⇔ (∀x)(x ∈ A ⇔ x ∈ B). Equivalent sets: A ~ B ⇔ n(A) = n(B). A wrong answer (e.g., "equivalent means same elements" or "equal means same number of elements") reveals confusion between the two concepts — the student is likely memorising terms without understanding the element-wise vs. cardinality distinction.

questions.q: Explain why every pair of equal sets is equivalent, but not every pair of equivalent sets is equal. Give a concrete counterexample for the converse.
questions.a: If A = B, they have identical elements, so n(A) = n(B) ⇒ A ~ B. Counterexample: A = {1,2,3}, B = {a,b,c} have n(A)=n(B)=3 ⇒ A ~ B, but 1 ∉ B ⇒ A ≠ B. A wrong explanation (e.g., "equal sets have same size so they are equivalent" without mentioning element identity) shows the student doesn't grasp that equality is a stronger condition requiring element-by-element matching.

questions.q: Let A = {x : x is a letter in the word "BANANA"} and B = {x : x is a letter in the word "ANANAB"}. Are A and B equal? Are they equivalent? Show your working.
questions.a: A = {B, A, N} (distinct letters), B = {A, N, B} = {A, B, N}. Elements are identical ⇒ A = B. n(A)=3, n(B)=3 ⇒ A ~ B. Both equal and equivalent. A student who writes A = {B,A,N,A,N,A} and B = {A,N,A,N,A,B} and says they are not equal because order/repetition differs has not internalised that sets ignore order and repetition.

questions.q: Let P = {x ∈ ℕ : x² < 20} and Q = {x ∈ ℕ : x is a prime factor of 30}. Determine whether P and Q are equal, equivalent, both, or neither. Justify.
questions.a: P = {1,2,3,4} (since 4²=16<20, 5²=25>20). Q = {2,3,5}. n(P)=4, n(Q)=3 ⇒ not equivalent ⇒ not equal. Neither. A student who miscalculates P as {1,2,3} (forgetting 4) or Q as {2,3,5,6} (including composite factors) makes arithmetic errors in set construction, not conceptual errors.

questions.q: A student claims: "If n(A) = n(B) = 5, then A = B because both have 5 elements." Evaluate this claim and provide a correct statement with a counterexample.
questions.a: The claim is false. Equal sets require identical elements, not just equal cardinality. Counterexample: A = {1,2,3,4,5}, B = {a,b,c,d,e}. n(A)=n(B)=5 but A ≠ B. Correct statement: "If A = B then n(A) = n(B), but the converse is not true." A student who agrees with the claim fundamentally confuses equivalence with equality.

questions.q: Construct two sets C and D, each with exactly 4 elements, such that C ~ D but C ≠ D. Use letters from the words "SCHOOL" and "COLLEGE" respectively. Write both sets in roster form.
questions.a: C = {S, C, H, O, L} from "SCHOOL" has 5 distinct letters. Need 4 elements. Choose C = {S, C, H, O} (any 4). D from "COLLEGE": distinct letters {C, O, L, E, G} = 5. Choose D = {C, O, L, E}. Then n(C)=4, n(D)=4 ⇒ C ~ D, but S ∈ C, S ∉ D ⇒ C ≠ D. A poor answer might use repeated letters or fail to ensure exactly 4 distinct elements, showing weak roster-form construction skill.
